question: Should newspapers have to warn people before publishing stories about their private lives?
answer: Damages come too late: once intimate details are printed, no court can unpublish them. A warning gives a judge the chance to weigh the public interest before the harm, not after. Max Mosley won his 2008 privacy case against the News of the World, yet the story had already been read by millions.
move: Whichever side you took, it turns on who can afford an injunction.
counterpoint: In Mosley's own case, the European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2011 that the law did not require prior notice. A warning invites an injunction, and the rich and powerful are best placed to obtain one, so the stories most worth telling about them would be the easiest to stop.
reference: European Court of Human Rights, Mosley v. the United Kingdom, application no. 48009/08, judgment of 10 May 2011
